title: Ang 1136–1156: Guru Arjan in Bhairao
tomorrow: what kind of wealth can't be tied up in a knot?

cards: Every form that asks your religion gives you boxes, and somewhere near the bottom there's one that says other, please specify.
On ang 1136, Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, writes a line that people have been specifying ever since. In paraphrase: I am not Hindu, nor Muslim; my body and breath belong to the One, Allah and Ram.
People still argue over it, at camps and kitchen tables. So what did he mean?

teach.b: Start with the whole hymn, because the line lands at the end of it. In paraphrase: I don't keep the fasts, nor Ramadan; I serve the One who protects me at the last. The one Lord, Gosain and Allah, is mine.
I don't go on pilgrimage to Mecca or to the holy rivers. I don't do the worship or the namaz; I bow to the One without form, in my heart. Then: not Hindu, not Muslim.
Sikh readers hear this in more than one way.
Some hear a line being drawn. The hymn sets aside the fasts, journeys and prayers of both paths around it and names a third thing: serve the One.
On this reading the Gurus' path is its own path, not a blend, and the line says so out loud.

Others hear a line being erased. The hymn calls the One by Hindu and Muslim names in the same breath, Gosain and Allah, Allah and Ram, and they hear the labels falling away before the One who has no form.
On this reading the hymn reaches toward both neighbors. Neither reading has to win today.

teach.h: WHERE THEY MEET: I SERVE THE ONE.
teach.b: Notice where they meet: the line both camps keep repeating is the one at the center.
I serve the One. Whatever box you tick, the hymn's question is who you serve.

how: Sikhs quote Guru Arjan's Bhairao hymn on ang 1136 in talks and kirtan; readers and teachers explain its closing line in more than one way, and the hymn is often read whole so the line keeps its setting.

o: where Kabir calls the Name a wealth he won't knot up
where the third Guru says the whole world is one clay
where Guru Arjan says he serves the One, not Hindu nor Muslim

games.q: the hymn on ang 1136 — tap the pairs.
p: two names for the one Lord
a line drawn: its own path
a line erased: the One past labels

s: Guru Arjan's hymn says all religions are the same
it sets aside both paths' fasts and pilgrimages and says: I serve the One. that's not the same claim.
the hymn calls the One by both Hindu and Muslim names
Gosain and Allah, Allah and Ram, in the same hymn.
Sikh readers all agree on what 'not Hindu, nor Muslim' means
some hear a distinct path; others hear the One beyond every label.

games.q: your cousin reads the line as 'Sikhs are their own path.' you read it as 'the One is past every label.' before you argue, what's the best case for your cousin's reading?
o: the hymn sets aside both neighbors' fasts, journeys and prayers, and names a third thing: serve the One.
the hymn says Hindus and Muslims both have it wrong, so somebody had to start over.
the hymn was written on the day the Sikh path was founded, as its first rule.
games.why: that's the strongest version of reading one, and it comes straight from the hymn. the hymn never says either neighbor is wrong, and nothing in it dates a founding.

practice: Say the center of the hymn out loud, slowly, in English: I serve the One. Then let the sit run quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru instead, a name Sikhs use for God.
If you'd like, read ang 1136 before you begin.
